<reason>Both sides argued competently, but CON (A) did the cleaner comparative work on the decisive clashes. A's distinction between the narrow, voluntary tracking prevention Safari/Firefox actually ship (funded partly by ad money) and the motion's "robust, system-level ad and tracker blocking" genuinely resolved B's strongest contradiction charge — B never fully answered why blocking ads, not just trackers, wouldn't affect the funding layer more. A's "who defines robust and who gets sued" pressure drew an answer from B (vendor discretion, performance obligation, TLS analogy), but B's answer remained soft, and A legitimately pressed it through closing. B's best material — the asymmetry between an unchosen surveillance default and a reversible switch, and the irreversibility of shipped profiles — was met by A's escalation-not-symmetry-breaking response and the point that individual opt-outs don't undo a statutory architecture. B's reach argument (webviews, school devices, children who never switch) stayed live but was narrowed to Chrome dominance, which A matched with a targeted antitrust remedy. A's clipped opening is a minor execution cost, but A's rebuttals progressed, answered pressure directly with proper A1/A2 format, and made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's rebuttal 2 (A4.3–A4.5): the observation that Safari and Firefox ship only narrow tracking prevention, not ad blocking, and survive on search-engine ad deals — this defused B's contradiction charge that "voluntary protection worked, so the mandate won't collapse services" and crystallized the narrow-vs-robust distinction that carried CON's closing.</best_rebuttal>
